meeting_header:
Date: 2026-07-14
Time: 15:00 - 15:45 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (CTO, Starlake), Daniel Kim (Lead ML Eng), Sarah Lopez (SRE)
Recording: yes
Notes: sales discovery for latency/throughput requirements for real-time scoring and streaming chat
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um quick intros then we'll jump in. I'm Maya from Redwood AE, and Liam our solutions engineer is here.
[00:07] Priya: thanks Maya, Priya here, CTO at Starlake. We have a short agenda: p95 targets, concurrency, and concrete numbers for tokens per second.
[00:15] Liam: great, quick question on scope — is this mostly realtime scoring on payments flows or chat assistants?
[00:22] Daniel: mostly realtime scoring, fraud scoring pipeline. We also have a small chat assistant but the critical path is scoring where p95 needs to be consistent.
[00:30] Sarah: our SRE also cares about burst windows; we can see spikes up to 600 concurrent requests for short periods.
[00:38] Maya: ok helpful. What p95 latency are you targeting?
[00:42] Priya: ideally sub-200ms p95 for short prompts (~32-64 tokens). For longer contexts (512 tokens) p95 under 600ms would be acceptable.
[00:53] Liam: got it; those targets make sense. For short prompts hosted infra can usually hit ~100-150ms p95 on optimized GPU instances, depending on the model. If you need predictable p95 with concurrency spikes, Dedicated or Private gives better isolation and reserved capacity so tail latency doesn't degrade.
[01:12] Daniel: what's the tradeoff cost-wise? We're a startup but processing millions of requests/month.
[01:18] Maya: hosted is usage-based so it's lowest upfront friction; Dedicated gives a monthly reserved pool which looks better for sustained high qps. Private (VPC/on-prem) is the largest commitment but required for compliance in some customers. We'll send a side-by-side.
[01:32] Priya: can you run us through token/sec benchmarking? We need to know how to translate our QPS into GPU needs.
[01:38] Liam: yes. We usually run a token-per-second benchmark with representative sequence lengths — short, medium, long. We produce tokens/sec and p95 generation latency numbers. For example, on a single A100 with quantized 4-bit weights you might see X tokens/sec for model A and Y for model B — but I'll attach concrete runs.
[01:56] Daniel: are you able to stream partial tokens back? Our pipeline prefers streaming for lower perceived latency.
[02:02] Liam: yes, Redwood supports streaming responses as well as chunked token streams. Streaming helps perceived latency but p95 for end-to-end completion can still be similar; for scoring you might not stream. For chat UX it's common.
[02:16] Sarah: curious about KV cache; we rely on context reuse for multi-turn.
[02:20] Liam: KV cache is supported, but note some transcriptions show K V cash etc, so docs clarify. We do prefix and KV caching to avoid recompute. Cache hits drastically increase tokens/sec effective throughput since you avoid full compute.
[02:35] Priya: in our workload ~60% of requests hit the same prefix in a user session, so caching would help a lot.
[02:40] Maya: that lines up; we can model effective cost savings if you share hit rate.
[02:45] Daniel: what about concurrency? Our 95th percentile concurrency during peaks is ~400, median more like 120. Can hosted handle that?
[02:54] Liam: hosted can autoscale, but autoscaling cold starts can impact p95 under sudden spikes. Dedicated reserved GPU pools give contiguous capacity and smoother p95 under load. For true hard SLOs we'd recommend Dedicated with autoscaling and burst capacity enabled.
[03:09] Priya: we also have strict compliance — SOC 2 and data residency in EU for some buckets. Private deployment might be necessary eventually.
[03:17] Maya: for compliance Redwood Private offers a VPC control plane and on-prem options; we can provide SOC2 report and a security checklist.
[03:25] Sarah: KMS integrations? We use AWS KMS and want envelope encryption.
[03:29] Liam: yes we integrate with customer KMS/HSM; we support envelope encryption and key rotation. We'll add the architecture note.
[03:36] Daniel: curious about model variants — do you fallback to smaller models on contention?
[03:40] Liam: yes smart routing can fallback to compatible variants (e.g., smaller quantized model) to preserve latency SLOs. That tradeoff is configurable per route.
[03:50] Priya: can you give an example of tokens/sec numbers? Rough ballpark is fine now.
[03:56] Liam: sure — rough illustrative numbers: on a single V100/16GB older card you might see ~40-60 tokens/sec for an L2-style model at 512 context; on A100 80-120 tokens/sec; on more optimized runtimes with quantization + fused kernels you can push 200-400 tokens/sec for shorter contexts. These are rough and model dependent.
[04:20] Daniel: so to meet sub-200ms p95 for 32 tokens we'd need to consider both per-request latency and concurrency. How do you size GPUs?
[04:28] Liam: we convert your QPS * average prompt length into tokens/sec requirement, then factor in concurrency and cache hit rate. Example: 200 RPS * 32 tokens = 6400 tokens/sec required; if one instance does 160 tokens/sec, you'd need ~40 instance-equivalents (or using batching or bigger cards to reduce count). We'll prototype with your traffic.
[04:50] Maya: also for scoring you can often batch multiple requests — Redwood runtime supports continuous batching which improves tokens/sec but may add a bit of latency.
[04:59] Daniel: how much added latency?
[05:02] Liam: depends on your SLO. Batching adds queuing time; at small batch windows (<10ms) overhead is minimal. We can tune batching parameters per-route to meet your p95.
[05:12] Priya: another question: what's the typical p95 difference between hosted and dedicated?
[05:16] Liam: hosted is elastic so p95 is good under steady load; under spikes you might see tail inflation if autoscale takes time. Dedicated gives predictability, so p95 tails are lower. I'd estimate 10-30% improvement in p95 tail for Dedicated in high-concurrency workloads.
[05:33] Sarah: do you provide per-token cost breakdowns so we can estimate spend?
[05:37] Maya: yes Redwood Console shows token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards. We'll share a sample export.
[05:44] Daniel: let's talk about the benchmark run — we can share a CSV with 1 week of traffic. What inputs do you need?
[05:51] Liam: ideally: seq len histogram, QPS over time (5m buckets), concurrency distribution, and sample payloads. We'll run token/sec and p95 generation latency for short/medium/long and streaming tests.
[06:05] Priya: perfect. Also want to check if we can do a canary with dedicated pool and fallback to hosted in case of issues.
[06:12] Liam: yes rollouts and canary A/B are supported; automatic fallback policies exist so you can route to hosted as fallback.
[06:20] Daniel: any caveats about quantization? We need high quality scores, so 4-bit might be ok but not degrade AUC.
[06:27] Liam: quantization can slightly affect model quality — we recommend running a quality regression on your eval set. Redwood Optimize will suggest quantization profiles by workload. For scoring we'd be cautious; usually quantize for less critical paths or run full-precision for core model.
[06:45] Priya: what about streaming? We rely on token-level streaming for chat; need to measure p95 for first token.
[06:52] Liam: we can measure time-to-first-byte (TTFB) and streaming latency; TTFB is often much lower than full completion latency. We'll include that in the benchmark.
[07:04] Maya: ok let's capture next steps — we'll send the pricing and benchmark harness, customer shares traffic. We'll schedule eng-to-eng bench.
[07:12] (crosstalk) Priya: quick — do you have SSO / SAML for the console?
[07:16] Maya: yes SSO/SAML and RBAC are supported; we'll include SSO docs.
[07:21] Sarah: also want audit logs retention options; we need 12 months for now.
[07:25] Liam: we have configurable audit log retention and can integrate with your SIEM.
[07:30] Daniel: for the bench run, do you need live traffic or can we replay logs?
[07:34] Liam: replay logs are fine and safer; if you want end-to-end streaming we'll do a limited live test during canary.
[07:42] Priya: what about data residency for EU customers?
[07:46] Maya: Redwood has regional control planes; for EU region we can keep data within EU and provide relevant assurances. For strict requirements Private may be needed.
[07:55] Daniel: any rough timeline for pilot? We could be ready in 2-3 weeks if benchmarks look good.
[07:59] Maya: that's feasible — pilot next week to run bench and then a 2-week dedicated pilot.
[08:06] Sarah: ok. Can you also list the specific model families you've tested for low-latency scoring?
[08:11] Liam: yes — we'll list curated open models and Redwood-verified performance profiles (we'll include names and cost/latency tradeoffs).
[08:19] Priya: thanks. Also curious about fallback behaviors — if model variant is incompatible for a route, will Redwood automatically choose a close variant?
[08:26] Liam: automatic fallback uses compatibility rules; in some edge cases manual mapping is required. We'll show examples.
[08:33] Daniel: final question — do you provide the benchmark harness as a repo? We prefer reproducible runs we can run in-house.
[08:38] Liam: yes the harness is a Github repo with scripts to produce tokens/sec and p95 numbers; we'll share access.
[08:44] Priya: perfect.
[08:46] Maya: great, recap of next steps: Maya send pricing + deck; Liam share harness + run baseline; Starlake provide traffic CSV; schedule 7/20 bench call. Anything else?
[08:58] Daniel: no that's it from me.
[09:00] Priya: thanks everyone.
[09:02] Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up in email.
[09:06] (end recording)
